final_recommendation: The negotiation failed to converge on a trilateral deal. Labor enforcement (30-day automatic sanctions, 13-14% wage credit) and auto rules (75% RVC) were locked between U.S. and Mexico, but Canada refused to move beyond 3.6-4.5% dairy market access while Congress demanded 5-6% on fluid milk and cheese as separate tariff lines. USTR confirmed a U.S.-Mexico bilateral could pass the House on auto/labor alone but needed dairy votes for a clean margin. Canada held its supply-management red line; the room ended with bilateral as the likely path and Canada negotiating dairy separately.
minority_objections: Canada repeatedly stated 5-6% on separate tariff lines would structurally break supply management, not just exceed a quota
Supply-chain manufacturers warned that sunset clause uncertainty would freeze investment regardless of dairy outcome
Labor union warned that threatening bilateral could lead to trading away enforcement in a future round to bring Canada back
key_conflicts: Canada's supply-management red line (3.6-4.5% max) vs. Congress's ratification floor (5-6% on fluid milk/cheese)
Whether 5-6% as 'separate tariff lines' within 3.6% overall ceiling was arithmetically coherent or political theater
Whether U.S.-Mexico bilateral had sufficient House votes to ratify without Canada's dairy concession
key_concessions: Mexico accepted 30-day automatic sanctions with no dispute panel delay (R4)
Canada moved from initial resistance to 13-14% wage credit acceptance (R2)
USTR conceded sunset review mechanism in year four instead of hard five-year termination (R5)
Canada offered 3.6% dairy access phased over time, then 4.5% within ceiling (R6-R7)
red_lines: Canada: supply management cannot absorb 5-6% on separate tariff lines without structural collapse
Congress: will not ratify at 3.6% dairy access—needs 5-6% on fluid milk and cheese for House votes
Labor union: 30-day automatic sanctions non-negotiable, no panel veto
ignored_or_underweighted_risks: Sunset clause investment freeze—raised repeatedly by supply-chain manufacturers but never integrated into the dairy/labor negotiation
Whether 'separate tariff lines' within an overall ceiling was arithmetically possible or just messaging—never clarified
Chapter 19 dispute settlement—Canada mentioned it once (R7) as needing confirmation but it was never addressed
Implementation timeline and compliance costs for 75% RVC—auto industry raised measurement questions (R1) that were never answered
downstream_risk_variables: If bilateral proceeds, Canada negotiates dairy alone under time pressure with reduced leverage
Sunset review mechanism details unspecified—could still freeze investment if review criteria unclear
Labor enforcement monitoring capacity in Mexico not detailed—independent monitors accepted in principle but operational structure undefined
Auto supply-chain re-sourcing costs and timeline for 75% RVC compliance never quantified
uncertainty_notes: The negotiation ended without resolution on whether a U.S.-Mexico bilateral would actually proceed or whether Canada would be given more time to move on dairy. The 5-6% vs. 3.6-4.5% gap remained unbridged. It is unclear whether 'separate tariff lines within an overall ceiling' was a real compromise or accounting fiction. Chapter 19 dispute settlement was mentioned by Canada but never negotiated. Sunset review mechanism was conceded in principle but operational details were not specified.

marker_evidence.auto_rules_bottleneck: 75% RVC and wage credit structure dominated R1-R2; Canada's ability to join trilateral hinged on resolving 13-14% vs 15-18% wage credit gap; drove Mexico-U.S. lock before Canada decision
marker_evidence.labor_enforcement_key: 30-day automatic sanctions with no panel delay became the locked floor that Congress and labor union made non-negotiable for ratification (R3-R4); Mexico's acceptance of this was the condition for proceeding
marker_evidence.canada_dairy_final_issue: 5-6% vs 3.6-4.5% dairy gap was the unresolved blocking issue that prevented trilateral signature; Congress confirmed it was needed for clean ratification; Canada refused to move beyond 4.5%
marker_evidence.dispute_settlement_canada_redline: Canada mentioned Chapter 19 once in R7 asking for confirmation it wouldn't move in bilateral, but it was never discussed, negotiated, or treated as a red line by any party
marker_evidence.sunset_to_review_compromise: USTR conceded year-four review mechanism (R5) in response to supply-chain concerns, but it did not change the negotiation outcome—dairy deadlock remained the blocking issue
marker_evidence.ratification_risk: Congress's vote-count requirements directly shaped the 5-6% dairy demand and the decision to threaten bilateral; USTR confirmed bilateral could pass but dairy votes mattered for clean margin (R7)
marker_evidence.supply_chain_adjustment: Raised multiple times by supply-chain and auto industry (R1, R5, R6, R7) as concern about re-sourcing costs and investment freeze, but never integrated into the final trade-offs—acknowledged but not decisive
marker_evidence.us_mexico_first_pressures_canada: U.S.-Mexico locked 75% RVC, 13-14% wage credit, and 30-day sanctions first (R2-R4), then used that as take-it-or-leave-it baseline to pressure Canada on dairy; bilateral threat was credible leverage throughout R5-R7
